title: Minimum Sum of Squared Difference
summary: Given two arrays nums1 and nums2 of equal length, and integers k1 and k2, you can adjust each element in nums1 by at most k1 times and each element in nums2 by at most k2 times by adding or subtracting 1.
statement: Given two arrays nums1 and nums2 of equal length, and integers k1 and k2, you can adjust each element in nums1 by at most k1 times and each element in nums2 by at most k2 times by adding or subtracting 1. Calculate the minimum possible sum of the squared differences between corresponding elements of the modified arrays.
constraints: One operation increments or decrements one value in either array by one.
Use at most k1 operations on nums1 and k2 on nums2 to minimize the sum of squared pairwise differences.
Only the total k1+k2 matters because either side can reduce an absolute difference.
reference_solution:
def minimum_squared_difference(nums1,nums2,k1,k2):
    differences=[abs(a-b) for a,b in zip(nums1,nums2)];operations=k1+k2
    if operations>=sum(differences):return 0
    low=0;high=max(differences)
    while low<high:
        middle=(low+high)//2
        if sum(max(0,value-middle) for value in differences)<=operations:high=middle
        else:low=middle+1
    cap=low;used=sum(max(0,value-cap) for value in differences);remaining=operations-used
    answer=sum(min(value,cap)**2 for value in differences)
    return answer-remaining*(2*cap-1)

hints: Convert each pair to an absolute difference and combine the two operation budgets.
Convex squares make reducing a currently larger difference never worse than reducing a smaller one.
Binary-search the smallest cap reachable within the budget, cap every difference, then distribute leftover reductions across cap-valued entries.
Leveling implements the repeated-largest greedy choice in bulk; reducing a cap to cap-1 lowers its square by 2*cap-1.
